title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident involves a coordinated attempt to manipulate AI systems by flooding them with fabricated source material. A front organization presented itself as a legitimate American think tank, publishing a large volume of pseudo-academic content in a short period, explicitly on a platform designed to optimize content for AI ingestion. The goal was not to persuade human readers directly but to shape the outputs of AI chatbots by seeding the information environment those systems draw from or are trained on.

The failure mode here is not one inside a model but upstream of it, in the data environment the model depends on. AI systems that rely on retrieving or learning from web-accessible content have no built-in mechanism to verify the institutional reality behind a source, only its surface features such as citations, formatting, and apparent provenance. A source that mimics academic conventions can pass the heuristics a model uses to weight credibility, which is precisely what this operation appears to have exploited.

What is not established is whether this content has materially altered any specific AI system's outputs, or whether the campaign achieved its stated influence objectives. The registration as foreign agent material with the U.S. Justice Department is a reported fact, but the legal and political consequences of the operation are not described in the reporting.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

A fake American think tank funded by the Israeli government published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days, designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots to generate pro-Israel arguments. The Hanover Institute for Public Policy, which does not exist as a legal entity, presented material on topics including Palestinian torture and Gaza aid shortages in a pseudo-academic format with carefully sourced citations. The site was built on a platform promising to optimize content for AI systems and was registered with the U.S. Justice Department as foreign agent material distributed for the Israeli government.

The operation represents part of a broader multimillion-dollar campaign financed by Israel and routed through European advertising firm Havas Media to manipulate AI training data and chatbot responses. Israeli officials have privately expressed frustration that despite spending tens of millions on public diplomacy efforts, American public support for Israel has declined significantly, with polling showing only 36 percent of Americans now sympathize with Israel. Experts warn the campaign demonstrates a new reality where foreign governments and others attempt to poison AI training data, making misinformation harder to fact-check.
